title: Cartesian coordinate system and quadrants
goal: Explain and apply cartesian coordinate system and quadrants in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Cartesian coordinates are ordered pairs (x,y). The signs of the coordinates determine quadrants I through IV; points on axes are not in a quadrant.
method: Mark x horizontally and y vertically, then locate the ordered pair. Coordinate sign conventions must be consistent.
guardrail: Axis points have no quadrant.

title: Distance and midpoint in 2D
goal: Explain and apply distance and midpoint in 2d in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: The distance between two points follows the Pythagorean theorem; a midpoint averages corresponding coordinates.
method: Subtract matching coordinates, square the differences and take the square root.
guardrail: Use the same coordinate units on both axes.

title: Section formula and division of a segment
goal: Explain and apply section formula and division of a segment in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: A point dividing a segment internally in the ratio m:n is a weighted average of the endpoints.
method: For AP:PB=m:n, use P=(nA+mB)/(m+n) coordinatewise.
guardrail: The ratio must be directed correctly; external division uses a different formula.

title: Slope and inclination of a line
goal: Explain and apply slope and inclination of a line in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: The slope measures vertical change per horizontal change; inclination θ gives m=tan θ when the line is not vertical.
method: Apply m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), checking for a zero denominator.
guardrail: Vertical lines have undefined slope, not slope zero.

title: Parallel and perpendicular slopes
goal: Explain and apply parallel and perpendicular slopes in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Parallel distinct nonvertical lines share slopes; perpendicular nonvertical lines have slopes whose product is −1.
method: For a perpendicular line use m₂=−1/m₁; treat vertical/horizontal lines separately.
guardrail: Do not use negative-reciprocal arithmetic for a zero or undefined slope.

title: Point-slope and slope-intercept line equations
goal: Explain and apply point-slope and slope-intercept line equations in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Point–slope form describes a line through a known point; slope–intercept form exposes slope and y-intercept.
method: Substitute (x₁,y₁) and m into y−y₁=m(x−x₁) and rearrange as needed.
guardrail: Point–slope form with a finite m does not represent a vertical line.

title: Two-point and general line equations
goal: Explain and apply two-point and general line equations in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: A line through two distinct points can be expressed as an equivalent standard or general equation Ax+By+C=0.
method: Find a direction or slope from the points, then rearrange; verify by substituting both endpoints.
guardrail: Two identical points do not determine a unique line.

title: Distance from a point to a line
goal: Explain and apply distance from a point to a line in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: The perpendicular distance from a point to a general-form line is the absolute value of the line expression divided by the normal length.
method: Put the line into Ax+By+C=0, then calculate |Ax₀+By₀+C|/√(A²+B²).
guardrail: The line coefficients A and B must not both be zero.

title: Intersections of two lines and angles between lines
goal: Explain and apply intersections of two lines and angles between lines in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Two nonparallel straight lines meet at one point, found by solving simultaneous equations. Angles can also be obtained from their direction vectors.
method: Equate slope–intercept forms or eliminate a variable; check for parallel or coincident lines.
guardrail: Parallel distinct lines do not have an intersection point.

title: Locus equations and analytic proofs
goal: Explain and apply locus equations and analytic proofs in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: A locus is the set of all points satisfying a geometric condition; its equation translates that condition into coordinates.
method: Set squared distances equal to avoid radicals; simplify and inspect extraneous results if any.
guardrail: A locus equation must include all and only the points meeting the given condition.

title: Circle equation: standard and general form
goal: Explain and apply circle equation: standard and general form in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: A circle has all points at distance r from its center (h,k); completing the square converts general to standard form.
method: Complete squares in x and y, then read center and radius from the equation.
guardrail: A nonnegative radius squared is required for a real circle.

title: Tangents and secants of coordinate circles
goal: Explain and apply tangents and secants of coordinate circles in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: At a circle tangency point, the radius and tangent are perpendicular. An external tangent length uses a right triangle.
method: For external P, PT²=PC²−r²; confirm P is outside the circle.
guardrail: No real tangent segment from a point strictly inside the circle.

title: Parabola: vertex, focus, directrix, and equation
goal: Explain and apply parabola: vertex, focus, directrix, and equation in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: A standard horizontal parabola y²=4px has vertex at the origin, focus (p,0), and directrix x=−p.
method: Read 4p from the squared-variable form; distinguish horizontal and vertical axes.
guardrail: The sign of p determines the opening direction.

title: Ellipse: vertices, foci, axes, eccentricity
goal: Explain and apply ellipse: vertices, foci, axes, eccentricity in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: An axis-aligned ellipse has constant sum of distances to its two foci; the semiaxes obey c²=a²−b².
method: Identify the major axis, find a and b from denominators, then compute focal distance c.
guardrail: Require a≥b>0 and place foci on the major axis.

title: Hyperbola: foci, axes, and asymptotes
goal: Explain and apply hyperbola: foci, axes, and asymptotes in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: A hyperbola consists of points whose absolute difference of focal distances is constant; its focal relation is c²=a²+b².
method: Read a and b from the positive and negative denominator terms; find c and asymptotes.
guardrail: Hyperbola asymptote slopes depend on the transverse-axis orientation.

title: General second-degree equations and conic identification
goal: Explain and apply general second-degree equations and conic identification in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: The quadratic part Ax²+Bxy+Cy² determines the nondegenerate conic type via the discriminant Δ=B²−4AC.
method: Inspect A, B, C; then check degeneracy separately if needed.
guardrail: The discriminant alone does not guarantee a nondegenerate real conic.

title: Translation and rotation of conic axes
goal: Explain and apply translation and rotation of conic axes in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Translating axes shifts the origin; rotating axes changes coordinate components and can remove a mixed xy term.
method: For translated origin (h,k), use x'=x−h and y'=y−k; for rotation apply the full transformation.
guardrail: Do not confuse moving the axes with rotating a geometric figure.

title: Polar coordinates and conversions
goal: Explain and apply polar coordinates and conversions in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Polar coordinates describe position by radius r and angle θ; Cartesian and polar forms are related by trigonometry.
method: Compute x=r cos θ and y=r sin θ; use quadrant information when converting back.
guardrail: Polar representations are not unique and negative radii require care.

title: Parametric curves and parametric equations
goal: Explain and apply parametric curves and parametric equations in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Parametric equations express coordinates as functions of a common parameter, useful for lines and curves.
method: Substitute the specified t; eliminate t only if a Cartesian relation is required.
guardrail: Different parameter intervals can trace different portions or orientations of the same curve.

title: Geometric vectors and vector operations
goal: Explain and apply geometric vectors and vector operations in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: A geometric vector has magnitude and direction; sum and difference are computed componentwise in a common basis.
method: Add corresponding components and calculate magnitude with the Euclidean norm.
guardrail: A vector is not just a point; displacement is independent of the choice of origin.

title: Dot product, cross product, and direction cosines
goal: Explain and apply dot product, cross product, and direction cosines in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: The dot product yields a scalar and tests orthogonality; the cross product in 3D yields a perpendicular vector.
method: Dot product: multiply matching components then sum; cross product: compute the determinant consistently.
guardrail: Dot and cross products are different operations; a zero dot product means orthogonal for nonzero vectors.

title: 3D Cartesian distance and midpoint
goal: Explain and apply 3d cartesian distance and midpoint in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Distance and midpoint formulas extend to three perpendicular Cartesian coordinate axes.
method: Compute the squared differences in x, y, z and take their square-root.
guardrail: Coordinates must be measured in consistent units.

title: Lines in space and parametric line equations
goal: Explain and apply lines in space and parametric line equations in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: A spatial line is described by a point and a nonzero direction vector, often parametrically.
method: Write (x,y,z)=(x₀,y₀,z₀)+t(a,b,c) and substitute the parameter.
guardrail: At least one direction component must be nonzero.

title: Planes in three-space and normal vectors
goal: Explain and apply planes in three-space and normal vectors in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: A plane is determined by a point and a nonzero normal vector; its equation is Ax+By+Cz+D=0.
method: Use the dot product of the normal with displacement from a known point or substitute to solve a missing coordinate.
guardrail: A,B,C must not all vanish.

title: Equation of a sphere in three-space
goal: Explain and apply equation of a sphere in three-space in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: The points in space at a fixed distance r from (h,k,l) form a sphere.
method: Read the squared radius and center from standard form, completing squares if needed.
guardrail: A negative right-hand side gives no real sphere.

title: Quadric surfaces: ellipsoids, paraboloids, hyperboloids
goal: Explain and apply quadric surfaces: ellipsoids, paraboloids, hyperboloids in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Quadratic equations in x,y,z describe quadric surfaces; squared-term signs and constants distinguish ellipsoids, paraboloids and hyperboloids.
method: Inspect a standard equation and intercepts/traces rather than guessing from a sketch.
guardrail: A quadratic form can represent a degenerate or imaginary surface for some constants.

title: Analytic area and coordinate-based geometry proofs
goal: Explain and apply analytic area and coordinate-based geometry proofs in coordinate geometry calculations and interpretations.
concept: Coordinate area follows from signed cross-products; the shoelace formula extends triangle calculations to simple polygons.
method: Order vertices consistently around the polygon, multiply diagonal coordinate pairs, subtract and divide by two.
guardrail: The listed vertices must follow the polygon boundary without self-crossing.
